title: New Decade-Long Study Finds H-1B Workers Paid 15% Less Than Peers
excerpt: Harvard economist George Borjas's analysis of 2014–2024 records finds visa holders better educated but underpaid — though critics say the wage gap is far smaller than claimed.
body:
• Harvard economist George Borjas analyzed a decade of U.S. immigration records and found H-1B workers are more educated than comparable American workers yet earn 15% to 16% less.
  • His labor-demand model puts the revenue-maximizing one-time visa fee at $97,000 to $154,000 — enough to raise $6.2 to $22.4 billion with little effect on employer demand.
  • Economists Jiaxin He and Adam Ozimek dispute the numbers: after fixing a mismatch that compares 2020 H-1B wages with 2023 native wages, they say the gap shrinks to about 5%.
  • On H-1B now: the underpayment concentrates among workers over 34 — the two-thirds of lottery winners aged 33 or younger earn a premium over comparable natives. The Trump administration's $100,000 H-1B petition fee is blocked by a federal judge in Oakland and is not being collected.

A new peer-reviewed analysis of a decade of U.S. immigration records has found that H-1B workers are better educated than comparable American workers but paid substantially less — a conclusion landing in the middle of the most heated fight over the visa program in years.

The study, "Overeducated and Underpaid: Characteristics of H-1B Visa Holders from New Administrative Records, 2014–2024," was written by Harvard economist George Borjas and published in Sage Journals. An earlier version circulated as a National Bureau of Economic Research working paper in February 2026.

What the study found

Borjas merged administrative data — I-129 petitions, which report the wage offer made to specific H-1B beneficiaries — with the American Community Survey, the Census Bureau's annual demographic survey. The combination gave him a decade-long view of the characteristics of actual visa holders against comparable native-born workers.

"The study, "Overeducated and Underpaid: Characteristics of H-1B Visa Holders from New Administrative Records, 2014–2024," was written by Harvard economist George Borjas and published in Sage Journals."

https://x.com/OwenGregorian/status/2106356753671635009

The headline finding: H-1B workers earn 15 to 16 percent less than comparable natives. The program, capped at 85,000 visas a year for for-profit firms with six-year terms, draws workers who are on average more educated than their American counterparts — hence "overeducated and underpaid."

Borjas then ran the data through a labor-demand model to simulate what happens if the government charges employers a one-time fee for each visa. For moderate levels of excess demand, the revenue-maximizing fee lands between $97,000 and $154,000 — a figure that would generate between $6.2 and $22.4 billion while having little or no effect on the number of H-1Bs hired. The fee would also change the skill mix, he found, making the workforce more skilled. Demand for the visas remains strong even if firms offshore some of the jobs.

The challenge to the findings

Not everyone accepts the 15 percent figure. In a February analysis, economists Jiaxin He and Adam Ozimek of the Economic Innovation Group argued that Borjas's comparison contains a critical flaw: a temporal mismatch between his two samples. The H-1B petitions span 2020 to 2023, while the native-born survey data cover 2023 alone.

With 15.1 percent inflation and an 18.7 percent wage increase for software occupations between 2020 and 2023, they wrote, the study is effectively comparing 2020 wages with 2023 prices — a comparison that mechanically inflates the gap. After correcting for the timing mismatch and comparing workers by place of work rather than mixing work and residence geographies, He and Ozimek put the true gap at about 5.3 percent, roughly one-third of Borjas's estimate.

The corrected data also reveal an age split that matters for workers. H-1B holders aged 21 to 22 earn a 20 percent wage premium over comparable natives, and the two-thirds of lottery winners who are 33 or younger earn more than their American counterparts. The negative gap only emerges after age 34.

Why it matters now

The debate is not academic. The Trump administration has moved to impose a $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions, and Borjas's model — which says employers will pay a six-figure fee without cutting hiring — is the intellectual backbone of the pro-fee case. Two federal judges have blocked the fee, most recently in Oakland, keeping it from being collected while the legal fight continues.

For Indian professionals, the largest group of H-1B beneficiaries, the stakes are direct: the fee's fate and the wage debate will shape how many engineers and researchers U.S. employers sponsor in the coming years.

What to watch

The immediate question is the court battle over the $100,000 fee. Beyond it, watch whether regulators or Congress cite the new administrative data in any fee rulemaking, and how the age-split findings — young H-1B workers out-earning natives — influence the political argument that the program systematically undercuts American wages.
